paragraphs.text: A [red tea](red:definition) made in 1979 at Shuishalian (水沙蓮), a locality in the Sun Moon Lake basin of Yuchi, Nantou. Red tea is what English calls black tea: the fully oxidised leaf, named in Chinese for the colour of the cup. Yuchi is where [Taiwan's red tea began](red:history), in the Japanese period, so this leaf comes from the place where the island's red tea started.

Forty-seven years is a long time for this kind of tea. Red tea has [no tradition of ageing](red:ageing). It is made to be drunk fresh, and sealed it holds its quality for about a year and a half to three years. A leaf from 1979 that has been kept this long sits well outside the style's usual life.

brewing.text: Red tea takes water near the boil, about 90 to 100°C; hotter water draws out its aroma and flavour more fully, but its bitterness faster too. In a pot or mug, use about a rounded spoon of leaf for each cup and steep three to five minutes, less for broken leaf and a little less, and a little cooler, for a light, delicate tea. Left too long, it turns bitter and drying, because time and heat pull more tannins from the leaf.

notice.text: A sweet cup, often with honey, floral or fruity notes, malt in many, and a brisk strength in the stronger teas. The liquor runs red, bright to deep.
